blocks.text: In a section of the pancreas the same organ shows two kinds of gland: acini that pour digestive enzymes into a duct leading to the duodenum, and small pale islands of ductless cells that release insulin into capillaries. Telling these apart, and knowing how each cell releases its product, is basic glandular histology.

blocks.markdown: Glands are epithelial structures. **Exocrine glands** keep a **duct** connecting them to the surface epithelium from which they developed and deliver secretion to a surface or lumen. **Endocrine glands** lose that connection (they are ductless); their products enter the interstitial fluid and then fenestrated capillaries. Exocrine glands are also described by the shape of their secretory unit (tubular or acinar) and whether the duct branches (simple or compound). **Myoepithelial cells** around many exocrine units contract to expel secretion.

blocks.title: Core definitions
blocks.text: An exocrine gland has secretory units plus a duct system delivering product to a surface or lumen. An endocrine gland is ductless and delivers hormone to the blood. A unicellular exocrine gland is a single secretory cell, such as a goblet cell.

rows: Secretory units (acini or tubules) plus ducts
Cords, clumps or follicles beside rich fenestrated capillaries
Thyroid, adrenal cortex, pituitary, pancreatic islets
blocks.caption: Exocrine versus endocrine glands

blocks.title: Classifying a gland from a section
blocks.prompt: A section shows rounded cell clusters with a central lumen draining into small ducts, and the product enters the duodenum. Classify the gland.

steps.text: Clusters around lumens with draining ducts show a duct system.
Delivery into the duodenal lumen is delivery to a lumen, not to blood.
So it is exocrine; these are the acinar secretory units of the pancreas.

blocks.markdown: **Modes of secretion.** In **merocrine** secretion, vesicles fuse with the apical plasma membrane (exocytosis) and the cell stays intact; examples are the pancreatic acinar cell, salivary glands and goblet cells. In **apocrine** secretion, the apical cytoplasm containing product is pinched off; the lipid droplets of the lactating mammary gland and the apocrine sweat glands of the axilla are classic examples (milk proteins are released by exocytosis, so the mammary gland uses more than one mode). In **holocrine** secretion, whole cells mature, fill with product and disintegrate to form the secretion; the sebaceous gland, which releases sebum into a hair follicle, is the classic example.

rows: Pancreatic acinar cell, salivary gland, goblet cell
Apical cytoplasm pinched off with product
Lactating mammary gland lipid, axillary apocrine sweat gland
Whole cell disintegrates and becomes the product
blocks.caption: Modes of secretion

blocks.title: Matching mode to mechanism
blocks.prompt: A pancreatic acinar cell releases zymogen granules by fusion with its apical membrane and remains intact. Name the mode.

steps.text: Granules fusing with the apical membrane is exocytosis.
No cytoplasm or cell is lost, which is merocrine secretion.

blocks.markdown: **Serous and mucous cells (H&E).** A **serous cell** makes a watery, protein- and enzyme-rich product: it has a round nucleus, basophilic basal cytoplasm (abundant rough ER) and pink apical secretory granules; the parotid gland and pancreatic acini are serous. A **mucous cell** makes mucins, glycoproteins that are poorly stained by H&E, so it looks pale or foamy with a flattened nucleus pushed to the base; the sublingual gland and goblet cells are mucous. In the submandibular gland, mixed units show mucous cells capped by a crescent of serous cells (a serous demilune).

items: Exocrine: ducts, product to surface or lumen. Endocrine: ductless, product to blood.
Merocrine: exocytosis; apocrine: apical cytoplasm lost; holocrine: whole cell lost.
Serous: dark basal cytoplasm, apical granules, round nucleus. Mucous: pale foamy cytoplasm, flat basal nucleus.

blocks.title: Do not confuse product type with mode of release
blocks.text: Serous versus mucous describes the product and the cell's appearance, whereas merocrine, apocrine and holocrine describe how it leaves the cell. Goblet cells, for example, are mucous cells that secrete by exocytosis.

points: Exocrine glands have ducts and deliver to a surface or lumen; endocrine glands are ductless and release hormone into the blood.
Merocrine (exocytosis, e.g. pancreatic acinus), apocrine (apical loss, e.g. mammary lipid and axillary sweat gland) and holocrine (whole cell, e.g. sebaceous gland) are the modes of release.
Serous cells are dark and granular; mucous cells are pale, foamy with flattened basal nuclei.

questions.stem: A section shows cords of cells packed against fenestrated capillaries with no ducts, and the product is a peptide hormone. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is an endocrine gland releasing product into interstitial fluid and then capillaries
It is an exocrine gland because its cells are epithelial
It is an exocrine gland because capillaries supply it
It is a holocrine gland because it lacks ducts

questions.correctOptionText: It is an endocrine gland releasing product into interstitial fluid and then capillaries

distractorRationale.b: Endocrine glands are also epithelial in origin.
distractorRationale.c: All glands have capillaries; ducts distinguish exocrine glands.
distractorRationale.d: Holocrine is a mode of release, not a lack of ducts.

questions.explanation: Absence of ducts and close association with fenestrated capillaries identify an endocrine gland. Holocrine describes a mechanism of release in exocrine glands, which is a separate question.

questions.stem: In the skin, cells at the periphery of a gland multiply, accumulate lipid as they move centrally, and finally disintegrate, releasing sebum into a hair follicle. Which mode of secretion is this?

options.text: Holocrine
Merocrine
Apocrine
Endocrine

distractorRationale.c: Apocrine loses only the apical cytoplasm.
distractorRationale.d: Endocrine refers to delivery into blood.

questions.explanation: Whole-cell disintegration is holocrine secretion, and the sebaceous gland is the classic example. The cells must be replaced continuously by division at the periphery.

questions.stem: Which pairing of gland and mode of secretion is correct?

options.text: Lactating mammary gland lipid droplets, apocrine
Sebaceous gland, merocrine
Parotid acinar cell, holocrine
Goblet cell, apocrine

questions.correctOptionText: Lactating mammary gland lipid droplets, apocrine

distractorRationale.c: Parotid acinar cells release by exocytosis (merocrine).
distractorRationale.d: Goblet cells release mucin by exocytosis (merocrine).

questions.explanation: Milk lipid leaves the cell enclosed in apical cytoplasm and membrane, the apocrine pattern. The other pairings reverse the classic examples.

questions.stem: A section of the submandibular gland shows units of cells with pale foamy cytoplasm and flattened basal nuclei, capped by crescents of cells with round nuclei, basophilic bases and pink apical granules. What do the crescents represent?

options.text: Serous cells forming demilunes over mucous cells
Myoepithelial cells forming ducts
Mucous cells compressed by the lumen
Endocrine cells of an islet

questions.correctOptionText: Serous cells forming demilunes over mucous cells

distractorRationale.b: Myoepithelial cells are flat and lie around units.
distractorRationale.c: Mucous cells are pale with flat basal nuclei.
distractorRationale.d: The tissue is an exocrine gland.

questions.explanation: Round nuclei, basophilic bases and apical granules mark serous cells, and the pale foamy cells with flattened basal nuclei are mucous. Serous demilunes capping mucous units are typical of mixed glands such as the submandibular.

questions.stem: True or false: endocrine glands retain a duct connecting them to the epithelium from which they developed.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Endocrine glands lose their duct connection during development and secrete into interstitial fluid and capillaries. It is exocrine glands that retain ducts.

questions.stem: In a pancreatic section, islets of pale cells lie among darker acini. Which statement correctly describes delivery of products?

options.text: Acini deliver enzymes through ducts to the duodenum; islets release hormones into capillaries
Both acini and islets deliver through the pancreatic duct
Acini release hormones into blood; islets deliver enzymes through ducts
Both acini and islets release directly into capillaries

questions.correctOptionText: Acini deliver enzymes through ducts to the duodenum; islets release hormones into capillaries
questions.explanation: The pancreas contains both an exocrine part (acini with ducts) and an endocrine part (islets). Ducts distinguish them in section.

questions.stem: Explain merocrine, apocrine and holocrine secretion and give a histological example of each.
markingGuide: Merocrine: exocytosis with the cell intact; example pancreatic acinar cell, salivary gland or goblet cell.
Apocrine: apical cytoplasm pinched off with the product; example lactating mammary lipid or axillary apocrine sweat gland.
Holocrine: whole cell disintegrates to form the secretion; example sebaceous gland.
Distinguishes mode of release from endocrine or exocrine delivery.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is how much of the cell is lost. Each mode needs a correct named example.

questions.stem: Describe how serous and mucous secretory cells differ on a routine H&E section and explain why mucous cells look pale.
markingGuide: Serous cells: round nucleus, basophilic basal cytoplasm, apical pink secretory granules.
Mucous cells: pale foamy cytoplasm with flattened basal nuclei.
Mucins are glycoproteins that stain poorly with H&E.
Serous products are protein and enzyme rich, e.g. parotid; mucous e.g. sublingual or goblet cells.
questions.explanation: The appearance reflects the product: abundant rough ER and granules in serous cells and poorly stained mucin droplets in mucous cells.

questions.stem: A goblet cell in the colon releases mucin granules by fusion with its apical membrane. Which description is correct?

options.text: A unicellular exocrine gland with mucous product and merocrine secretion
An endocrine cell with serous product and holocrine secretion
A unicellular exocrine gland with serous product and apocrine secretion
A multicellular endocrine gland with mucous product and merocrine secretion

questions.correctOptionText: A unicellular exocrine gland with mucous product and merocrine secretion

distractorRationale.b: Goblet cells deliver to a lumen and are not endocrine.
distractorRationale.c: The product is mucin and release is by exocytosis.
distractorRationale.d: It is a single cell and exocrine.

questions.explanation: A goblet cell delivers mucin to a lumen, so it is exocrine, and its exocytosis makes it merocrine. This shows that product type and mode of release are separate classifications.

questions.stem: A blockage of a salivary duct causes swelling of the gland, whereas removal of a thyroid lobe does not cause such swelling but changes blood hormone levels. Explain both findings using the structural difference between exocrine and endocrine glands.
markingGuide: Exocrine glands deliver through a duct to a lumen or surface, so duct blockage causes secretion to back up.
Endocrine glands are ductless and release into interstitial fluid and capillaries.
Loss of endocrine tissue therefore alters circulating hormone levels rather than causing ductal obstruction.
Links structure (duct versus capillary route) to the findings.
questions.explanation: The duct is the exocrine delivery route and a blocked duct stops drainage, whereas endocrine output depends on capillary access and tissue mass.
